title: At COP31, Bangladesh puts its climate needs at $10-11 billion a year
excerpt: The delegation said the country spends $4.5-5 billion of its own money each year and that pledged finance is not turning into money on the ground.

image.alt: Delegates seated around the negotiating tables at the COP31 Presidency's energy ministerial meeting in Antalya, Türkiye, on 10 November 2026
image.credit: Necati Savas / European Union, 2026, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 4.0

content:
Bangladesh needs $10-11 billion a year to deal with climate change but spends only $4.5-5 billion from its own budget, its delegation told a press briefing in Antalya on Friday, 13 November, the fifth day of negotiations at COP31. The briefing was reported by The Business Standard.

Environment, Forest and Climate Change Minister Abdul Awal Mintoo said pledges of climate finance have run ahead of what is actually delivered. Foreign Affairs State Minister Shama Obaed Islam said the money should reach the communities that need it most.

What Bangladesh asked for

  • Faster delivery of international climate finance, with more grants for national adaptation plans.
  • Simpler, direct access to the Green Climate Fund, the Global Environment Facility and the Adaptation Fund.
  • More money, simpler access and faster payouts from the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage, covering economic and non-economic losses.
  • Backing for the Least Developed Countries group target of tripling adaptation finance to $120 billion a year before 2035.
  • Adaptation indicators that do not add reporting burdens, and more support for locally led adaptation.
  • Opposition to trade measures such as the EU Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism, which the delegation said could hurt exporters in developing countries.

New money on the table

The delegation said Bangladesh is expected to be one of the first five countries to receive up to $30 million each from the Climate Investment Funds. Details of the programme and timing were not given.

Why it matters

The $10-11 billion figure is the clearest statement yet from the new government of the gap it wants donors to fill. For NGOs, the push for direct access and locally led adaptation is the part to follow: it decides whether climate money reaches district and union level partners or stays with ministries and large intermediaries. Devlens reported on 13 November that the tripling target was kept off the formal agenda.

What to watch

The draft decisions on adaptation finance and loss and damage expected in the second week, and which Bangladeshi institutions are named to manage the Climate Investment Funds money.
